introduction.p: A continuous function need not be differentiable, and a derivative need not be continuous. These examples distinguish those properties and show why a sampled graph cannot establish differentiability.

subsection.p: This example is the motion version of a corner. The particle has a position at every nearby time. The position changes without a break. But the direction of motion changes too abruptly for there to be one instantaneous velocity at t=0.
There is a useful way to say the same thing with local linear approximation. If s were differentiable at 0, then near 0 we would have
for one fixed slope m. But for h>0, this would require m=1, while for h<0, it would require m=-1. One line cannot model both sides to first order.
The graph is unbroken, but it is not locally linear at the corner.

exercise.title: Why can a continuous position have no velocity at one instant?

statement.p: The motion s(t)=|t| never jumps, but at t=0 the particle reverses instantly. In your own words, why is continuity of position not enough for an instantaneous velocity, and why does one line fail as a local linear model there?

hint.p: Continuity controls nearby values. Differentiability controls nearby slopes. A single slope cannot be both 1 and -1.

note.title: Differentiable does not mean continuously differentiable
note.p: A function may have a derivative at a point even though the derivative function behaves badly near that point.

Continuity of the derivative is a stronger requirement than differentiability. The definition of a derivative does not by itself establish that f\prime is continuous.

exercise.title: Why can a derivative exist and still fail to be continuous?

statement.p: The function x^2\sin(1/x), extended by zero at the origin, is differentiable there, but its nearby derivative values do not approach f\prime(0). Explain the distinction between differentiability and continuity of the derivative.

hint.p: Differentiability at a point is a statement about one limit of difference quotients. Continuity of f' is a statement about the derivative function at nearby points.

subsection.title: A graphing calculator can miss a sharp corner
subsection.p: Graphs are useful, but a graph on a screen is not the function. A screen shows finitely many pixels. A calculator or computer often samples finitely many points and connects them. If the important feature lies between sampled points, the picture may miss it.

subsection.p: The lesson is not that calculators are bad. The lesson is that a picture is evidence, not proof. A graph can suggest where to look. The derivative definition decides what is true.

subsection.p: The warnings in this section protect the meaning of the derivative.

The derivative is now defined, interpreted, and tested. But computing every derivative from the limit definition is too slow. The next chapter builds a faster language: rules for differentiating sums, products, quotients, compositions, and the elementary functions.

exercise.title: Why is a graphing calculator not a proof of differentiability?

statement.p: A finite plot of |x-0.03| can miss the corner if that point is never sampled. In your own words, why can a picture hide a nondifferentiable point, and what test actually decides whether f'(a) exists?

hint.p: A screen shows finitely many samples. The difference quotient examines the point itself, from both sides if needed.
